The right answer on the ride is to read the placard and the handbook that belong to this serial number rather than quoting a figure from a later serial block.

q: What is the resultant that the wing actually has to support in a turn?
a: The vector sum of weight, acting straight down, and the inertial reaction to the turn, acting horizontally outward. That resultant is longer than weight alone and tilted outward, and the wing must produce lift equal and opposite to it, which is why total lift in a level turn exceeds weight by one over the cosine of the bank. The ratio of that resultant to the airplane's weight is precisely what load factor means.

q: How does the airplane's weight affect its glide ratio?
a: It does not. The glide ratio is the lift-to-drag ratio, which is a function of angle of attack and configuration alone, so a heavy airplane and a light one glide the same distance from the same height in still air. What changes is the speed at which that angle of attack occurs, which varies with the square root of weight, so the heavy airplane arrives sooner at a higher speed and a higher rate of descent.

q: What does a fixed-pitch propeller do to the power available at low airspeed?
a: It reduces it. The blade angle is set for one compromise condition, so at a low forward speed the blades meet the air at too large an angle, the propeller loads up, rpm falls and the engine cannot develop its rated power. That is why full-throttle static rpm on this airplane is specified well below the 2,700 rpm rated speed, and why slow, high-power flight regimes have less thrust available than the horsepower figure suggests.

q: Why does induced drag dominate at low speed and parasite drag at high speed?
a: Because they depend on speed in opposite ways. Induced drag is the price of making lift, and at low speed the wing needs a high angle of attack and makes strong tip vortices, so it varies inversely with the square of airspeed. Parasite drag is the cost of pushing the airframe through the air and varies with the square of airspeed. Their sum is a U-shaped curve whose minimum is lift-to-drag maximum, which is where the two are equal.

q: What is actually happening at the wing when it stalls?
a: The boundary layer can no longer follow the increasingly adverse pressure gradient over the upper surface, so the airflow separates and the low pressure region over the wing collapses. Lift falls sharply, drag rises sharply, and the separated wake over the tail produces the buffet that warns you. Nothing about airspeed is involved in the definition; the separation happens at the critical angle of attack whatever the airplane is doing.

q: Why does a wing's maximum lift coefficient put an absolute limit on turn performance?
a: Because the lift needed in a level turn goes up as one over the cosine of the bank, without limit, while the lift available at a given speed is capped by the maximum lift coefficient. Where the two meet is the steepest level turn the airplane can make at that speed, and it is set by the stall, not by the structure or the engine. Going steeper from there requires more airspeed, and eventually the structural limit becomes the binding one.

q: How does extending flaps change the lift curve and the stall?
a: Flaps increase the camber of the wing, which raises the lift coefficient at every angle of attack and raises the maximum lift coefficient, so the wing can carry its weight at a lower airspeed. They also reduce the angle of attack at which the stall occurs, measured against the original chord line, which is why the nose attitude at the stall is lower with flaps out. The later settings add far more drag than lift.

q: Does the ball tell you anything about the airplane's angle of attack?
a: No, and conflating the two is dangerous. The ball reports only whether the lateral forces are in balance, that is whether the airplane is slipping or skidding; it is blind to angle of attack, load factor and how near the wing is to stalling. A perfectly centered ball at the critical angle of attack is still a stall, and an uncoordinated one simply decides which wing will drop when that stall arrives.
